title: Pakistan's Business Community Alleges Silent Visa Ban by UAE as Export Losses Mount
excerpt: Pakistani officials confirm the UAE has halted most visa issuance for its nationals, threatening $6.3 billion in annual remittances and disrupting bilateral trade.
body:
• The UAE has effectively frozen visa issuance for Pakistani passport holders since March 2026, with only diplomatic and official passports exempted
  • Pakistani businesses report export losses and cancelled trade trips as travel agents cite up to 80% rejection rates on new visa applications
  • The UAE hosts 1.6 million Pakistanis — its second-largest expatriate community — and annual remittances exceed $6.3 billion
  • Officials warn a full passport ban would be difficult to reverse, as Pakistan's passport ranks among the world's weakest

Pakistan's business community is sounding the alarm over what it describes as a de facto visa ban by the United Arab Emirates, warning that the restrictions are choking bilateral trade and threatening the livelihoods of millions who depend on Gulf employment.

Though the UAE has not officially declared a ban, Pakistani officials have confirmed to the country's Senate Human Rights Committee that regular visa issuance for Pakistani nationals has been halted since late March 2026. The freeze covers tourist, employment, and business visa categories, leaving only holders of diplomatic and official blue passports unaffected.

Trade and Business Disruption

The restrictions have sent shockwaves through Pakistan's export sector. Business delegations scheduled for UAE trade shows have been cancelled, and manufacturers who rely on Gulf buyers report disrupted supply chains. Pakistani travel agents say visa applications are being systematically rejected, with some agencies reporting rejection rates as high as 80 percent.

"If a ban is imposed, getting it removed would be difficult."

— Salman Chaudhry, Additional Interior Secretary, Pakistan

Senator Samina Mumtaz Zehri, who chairs the Senate committee, confirmed that the UAE imposed the restrictions after repeated incidents of Pakistani nationals engaging in unlawful activities on its soil. She said only a handful of visas had been granted recently, "and those too after much difficulty."

Criminal Activity and Diplomatic Strain

The UAE's move stems from frustration over the misuse of visit visas by Pakistani nationals. In 2025, the UAE deported approximately 6,000 Pakistanis for visa violations and involvement in begging rings. Saudi Arabia deported another 24,000, bringing total Gulf Cooperation Council deportations of Pakistanis past 32,000 in a single year.

Reports from April 2026 allege that the crackdown has swept up not only labourers but also doctors, businessmen, and teachers. Pakistan's Interior Ministry has acknowledged the severity of the situation and initiated quiet diplomatic negotiations to prevent a complete passport ban.

Remittance Lifeline at Risk

The economic stakes extend far beyond trade. The UAE hosts approximately 1.6 million Pakistanis — the country's second-largest expatriate community after Indians — and remittances from the Gulf state crossed $6.3 billion in the 2024-25 fiscal year. With more than 800,000 Pakistanis applying for visas to Gulf nations annually, a prolonged freeze could strain Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves at a time when the country is already navigating fiscal fragility.

Job-seekers who traditionally enter the UAE on visit visas before converting to work permits face the steepest impact. Recruitment agencies report being flooded with refund requests from stranded applicants.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, Pakistan's visa crisis underscores the precarious nature of expatriate status in the region. Indian workers — who form the UAE's largest foreign community at over 3.5 million — have historically maintained stronger visa standing, but Gulf states' increasing willingness to impose blanket restrictions on entire nationalities is a reminder that policy shifts can reshape diaspora communities overnight.

What's Next

The UAE's ambassador to Pakistan has outlined steps to streamline visa processing, including online applications and e-visas. A new UAE Visa Centre in Pakistan processes roughly 500 applications daily. But on the ground, the gap between official reassurances and actual approvals remains wide. Islamabad is now pushing police verification reforms requested by Gulf states in hopes of restoring normal visa operations — but analysts caution that rebuilding trust could take months, if not longer.
